title: Assessing agricultural drought risk under CMIP6 scenarios using hybrid AI models and satellite-derived TVDI
abstract: Abstract This study focuses on predicting the temperature vegetation dryness index (TVDI), an agricultural drought index, for a Mango orchard in Tamale, Ghana, using climate projections and satellite imagery. The nonlinear cross-correlation between the standardized precipitation Index (SPI) and TVDI was examined to comprehend the impact of meteorological drought on agricultural drought. Historical precipitation data and CMIP6 projected data (2015–2050) from 35 climate models across four Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) scenarios were subjected to bias correction and utilized to compute SPI. TVDI was obtained from Landsat 8/9 imagery and validated by UAV-based data, demonstrating good agreement. Mutual information (MI) analysis revealed scenario-dependent lag times of 0-6 months between SPI and TVDI, facilitating lag-based prediction. A hybrid Wavelet-ANFIS/FCM model predicted TVDI using SPIs as inputs with high accuracy (RMSE < 0.08 in training and test phases). These findings demonstrate a progressive increase in the frequency and duration of agricultural drought under higher-emission SSP scenarios, underscoring the escalating future risk and emphasizing the necessity for an agricultural drought early warning system and climate adaptation planning. The proposed framework provides an AI-driven solution for predicting agricultural drought, supporting sustainable development goals (SDGs) related to food security and climate action.
problem: Existing studies lack an integrated framework for predicting future agricultural drought, often failing to use bias-corrected climate projections or account for the complex, nonlinear, and scenario-specific time lags between meteorological conditions and vegetation stress.
method: The paper proposes a hybrid AI framework using a Wavelet-ANFIS/FCM model to predict future agricultural drought (TVDI) based on its lagged, nonlinear relationship with meteorological drought (SPI) derived from bias-corrected CMIP6 climate projections and validated with satellite data.
task: The task is to predict a future agricultural drought index (TVDI) for a mango orchard in Ghana by using CMIP6 climate projections and satellite imagery as inputs for a hybrid AI model.

Changes in global climatic conditions, especially in arid and semi-arid regions, have altered precipitation patterns both temporally and spatially. This changes the frequency of hydrological extremes, including floods and droughts fundamentally¹.
Particularly in West African regions near the Sahel Zone, such as Tamale in northern Ghana, where farming is mostly rain-fed, drought impacts threaten food security and agricultural productivity.

Since the 1980s, remote sensing data, especially satellite imagery, have been applied for vegetation indices such as the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) and for land surface temperature (LST) estimations. The relationship between NDVI and LST has been used to track crop and orchard water stress through the temperature vegetation dryness index (TVDI). The TVDI measures a combined signal of both the soil moisture under trees and the leaf water status and has been considered as an agricultural drought index¹⁰. It can be calculated and validated using high-resolution multispectral and thermal data from Landsat 8 and 9 satellites, together with field-based methodologies such as thermal surveys conducted by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) ¹¹⁻¹³.
